14: # SKILL.md File Templates - Creation Guide
15: 
16: Templates for creating SKILL.md files with proper structure, frontmatter, and required sections.
17: 
18: ---
19: 
20: ## 1. OVERVIEW
21: 
22: ### Purpose of SKILL.md Files
23: 
24: SKILL.md files define AI agent skills - reusable capabilities that extend an agent's functionality for specific domains or workflows. A well-crafted SKILL.md:
25: 
26: - **Triggers automatically** when relevant patterns are detected
27: - **Guides the agent** through specialized workflows
28: - **Maintains consistency** across conversations
29: - **Encodes expertise** in specific domains
30: 
31: ### Template Overview
32: 
33: This guide provides **one comprehensive SKILL template** (Section 3) that covers all skill types from simple single-purpose tools to complex multi-mode orchestrators.
34: 
35: **The template is flexible:**
36: - **Simple skills**: Use required core sections only (WHEN TO USE, SMART ROUTING, HOW IT WORKS, RULES, REFERENCES)
37: - **Skills with bundled resources**: Say in Section 2 what selects the skill and what it loads first, and put the router in the sibling `ROUTER.md`. Use `references/`, `assets/`, and `scripts/`
38: - **Multi-mode skills**: Expand WHEN TO USE and HOW IT WORKS sections by mode
39: - **All skills**: Section 2 (SMART ROUTING) is required: 8 to 12 non-blank lines of plain prose
40: 
41: **Target size**: 800-2000 lines for SKILL.md (<5k words total)
42: 
43: **Examples**:
44: - Simple: Unit test generator, documentation formatter (no bundled resources)
45: - Moderate: API client, specialized code reviewer (with references and assets)
46: - Complex: Workflow orchestrator, document quality pipeline (multi-mode with extensive resources)
47: 
48: ### Progressive Disclosure Principle
49: 
50: SKILL.md architecture follows progressive disclosure:
51: 
52: 1. **Metadata** (YAML frontmatter) - Always in context (~100 words)
53: 2. **SKILL.md body** - When skill activates (<5k words)
54: 3. **Bundled resources** - Loaded as needed (unlimited size)
55: 
56: **Critical**: Keep SKILL.md <5k words. Move detailed content to `references/`, `scripts/`, or `assets/`.
57: 
58: ### Document Type Requirements
59: 
60: **Enforcement Level**: STRICT (SKILL.md files require perfect structure)
61: 
62: **Required Elements**:
63: - ✅ YAML frontmatter with required fields
64: - ✅ H1 title with subtitle
65: - ✅ Numbered H2 sections (ALL CAPS, integers only, never a letter suffix such as `2b.`)
66: - ✅ Section separators (`---`)
67: - ✅ No table of contents (forbidden in SKILL.md)
68: 
69: **Quality Targets**:
70: - Structure: 100/100
71: - Content quality: High (AI-evaluated)
72: - Overall: High (human/AI judgment)
73: 
74: ---
75: 
76: ## 2. FRONTMATTER REQUIREMENTS
77: 
78: ### Required Fields
79: 
80: | Field | Required | Format | Example |
81: |-------|----------|--------|---------|
82: | `name` | ✅ | hyphen-case | `my-skill-name` |
83: | `description` | ✅ | Single line, **≤ 130 chars** for skills (≤ 110 for commands), 1,536-char hard cap | `"Handles X when Y occurs"` |
84: | `allowed-tools` | ✅ | Array: `[Tool1, Tool2]` | `[Read, Write, Edit, Bash]` |
85: | `version` | ✅ | 4-part X.Y.Z.W | `1.0.0.0` |
86: 
87: > **Hard rules**: not a frontmatter key. They live in `hard-rules.json` beside the skill's `SKILL.md`, a JSON array of `{id, check, message, severity}` objects that the dispatch preflight reads.
88: 
89: > **Description budget & trim style**: see [`frontmatter-templates.md` § Description Budget & Trim Style](../../../sk-create-frontmatter/assets/frontmatter-templates.md).
90: > Keep total project descriptions under the ~6,400-character ceiling. This leaves headroom below the 8,000-character auto-discovery limit.
91: > Drop product and stack lists. Drop marketing prose. Keep the skill name, primary verb, domain noun and mode suffixes (`:auto` or `:confirm`).
92: 
93: ### Template
94: 
95: ```yaml
96: ---
97: name: sk-example
98: description: Example workflow skill demonstrating proper frontmatter format with specific capabilities, use cases, and key differentiators for AI agent discovery.
99: allowed-tools: [Read, Write, Edit, Bash, Glob, Grep]
100: version: 1.0.0.0
101: ---
102: ```
103: 
104: ### Key Rules
105: 
106: - **name**: Must match folder name exactly, hyphen-case only
107: - **description**: Third-person voice, single line, no `<>` brackets
108: - **allowed-tools**: Use brackets `[...]`, not comma-separated string
109: - **hard rules**: Not a frontmatter key. They live in `hard-rules.json` beside `SKILL.md`, a JSON array of `{id, check, message, severity}` objects the dispatch preflight reads.
110: 
111: > **Complete Reference**: For validation rules, edge cases, array formats, and all document type frontmatter, see [frontmatter-templates.md](../../../sk-create-frontmatter/assets/frontmatter-templates.md)
112: 
113: ---
114: 
115: ## 3. SKILL TEMPLATE (WITH BUNDLED RESOURCES)

117: **Use for**: Skills with bundled resources (references, scripts, or assets)
118: 
119: **Target**: 800-2000 lines (SKILL.md <1000 lines, rest in resources)

122: - Max 5000 words (3000 recommended)
123: - Max 3000 lines

439:   - Group related templates together
440:   - Example: `assets/skill/`, `assets/readme/`, `assets/flowcharts/`
441: - **scripts/** = Typically flat, but subfolders OK for large script collections

444: - Skills auto-discovered from `.skilled/skills/*/SKILL.md` frontmatter
445: - Skill name in frontmatter MUST match folder name
446: - Skills appear as `skills_<name>` functions in OpenCode (hyphens → underscores)

451: ## 4. SECTION-BY-SECTION CONTENT GUIDANCE
452: 
453: ### Section 1: WHEN TO USE
454: 
455: **Purpose**: Help the AI agent and users understand WHEN to activate this skill
456: 
457: **Section Boundary Rule**: "When to Use" = WHEN (triggers only). File references belong in Section 2 (Smart Routing).
458: 
459: **Essential Content** (ONLY these belong here):
460: - Activation triggers (what conditions activate this skill)
461: - Use case categories (2-4 categories)
462: - Specific scenarios (3-5 per category)
463: - Anti-patterns ("When NOT to Use")
464: - Keyword triggers (optional)
465: 
466: **Content that does NOT belong here** (move to Section 2 inline):
467: - ❌ File references
468: - ❌ Resource paths
469: - ❌ Resource tables
470: 
471: **Structure**:
472: 
473: ### Activation Triggers
474: 
475: **Use when**:
476: - [Specific scenario with context]
477: - [Specific scenario with context]
478: 
479: **Keyword Triggers**:
480: - [Pattern that activates skill]
481: 
482: ### Use Cases
483: 
484: ### [Use Case Category]
485: 
486: [Content for use case]
487: 
488: ### When NOT to Use
489: 
490: **Skip this skill when:**
491: - [Anti-pattern with rationale]
492: 
493: **Writing Tips**:
494: - Be specific: "Generate JSDoc for functions" not "document code"
495: - Include context: Why each scenario benefits from this skill
496: - Clear boundaries: Explicitly state what's out of scope
497: - Trigger patterns: What keywords/patterns auto-activate skill
498: - **NO file references** - those go in Section 2 (Smart Routing)
499: 
500: **Word Budget**: 100-200 lines
501: 
502: ---
503: 
504: ### Section 2: SMART ROUTING (Required for All Skills)
505: 
506: **Purpose**: Use this section to explain how you route a request to this skill's resources.
507: 
508: **Three skill kinds, one shape**:
509: 
510: | Kind | How to tell | What Section 2 says |
511: |------|-------------|---------------------|
512: | Hub | the folder holds `mode-registry.json` and `hub-router.json` | how a prompt reaches a mode, and where the root `ROUTER.md` is |
513: | Mode packet | a packet folder inside a hub | what selects this packet, what it loads first, and where its own `ROUTER.md` is |
514: | Standalone | neither hub file | the same as a mode packet, with the router in its own `ROUTER.md` |
515: 
516: **The limit**: 12 non-blank lines and 180 words are the hard ceilings the check enforces. Aim for 8 to 12 lines. A packet or standalone skill says three things: what selects it, what it loads first, and where the machine router is.
517: 
518: **The sibling router**: the machine router lives in `ROUTER.md` beside `SKILL.md`, under a final `## MACHINE ROUTER` heading.
519: That heading is the one every reader parses. Its section number is optional, so `## MACHINE ROUTER` and `## 9. MACHINE ROUTER` both count, and the check ignores the number.
520: Keep pseudocode out of SMART ROUTING and put it in that section.
521: `SKILL.md` carries no `## MACHINE ROUTER` section of its own: two homes for one router is the dual declaration the check reports.
522: 
523: **The link line**: Section 2 names the router file with a relative markdown link, [`ROUTER.md`](./ROUTER.md), and its target resolves on disk. A sentence that mentions the name without a link fails, because a reader cannot follow it to a file that is not there.
524: 
525: **One router per folder**: every skill and every mode packet owns `ROUTER.md` inside its own folder, linked from its own `SKILL.md`. A router file whose real path leaves the folder is not that skill's router.
526: 
527: **The no-match outcome** is named `UNKNOWN_FALLBACK` everywhere. Low confidence returns a disambiguation checklist, never an empty result and never a guess.
528: 
529: **Validation**: `package_skill.py --strict` reports the routing shape with five codes:
530: 
531: | Code | Finding |
532: |------|---------|
533: | `RS-001` | SMART ROUTING is longer than the limit (12 lines or 180 words by default) |
534: | `RS-002` | `SKILL.md` carries a `## MACHINE ROUTER` section, with or without a code block |
535: | `RS-003` | A `## MACHINE ROUTER` section is not the last H2 of the document that holds it |
536: | `RS-004` | the skill has no sibling `ROUTER.md`, or its real path leaves the skill folder |
537: | `RS-005` | `SKILL.md` has no relative markdown link to `./ROUTER.md` that resolves |
538: 
539: The machine block itself is a fenced block or an unfenced run of indented lines.
540: It declares the router with one of these markers: `INTENT_SIGNALS =`, `RESOURCE_MAP =`, `DEFAULT_RESOURCE =`, `UNKNOWN_FALLBACK_CHECKLIST =`, `def discover_markdown_resources` or `def _guard_in_skill`.
541: A fence closes only on a run of the same character that is at least as long as its opening run.
542: 
543: **Known debt** is listed in `sk-create-skill/scripts/routing-shape-known-debt.json`.
544: Entries use skill paths relative to `.skilled/skills`, such as `sk-code/sk-code-review`.
545: A folder outside that root is never debt.
546: Each entry records `{"lines", "words", "machineBlocks", "codes"}`.
547: A listed skill fails if its line count, word count or machine blocks left in `SKILL.md` exceed the record, or if it adds an unrecorded code.
548: The checker ignores entries in any other form.
549: Remove an entry when the skill follows the canon.
550: 
551: **Placement**: the SMART ROUTING section sits after Section 1 (WHEN TO USE) and before HOW IT WORKS, and `ROUTER.md` sits beside `SKILL.md` at the skill root.
552: 
553: **Worked example** (a canon Section 2 and its sibling router, nothing else):
554: 
555: \## 2. SMART ROUTING
556: 
557: Use this skill for [domain] work: [trigger 1], [trigger 2], or [trigger 3].
558: The first signal is [project/stack/mode detection], because it picks the knowledge folder before any intent scoring.
559: Load `references/[default].md` first on every run. The other files assume it.
560: Then load what the matched intent maps to: [intent A] reads `references/[domain]/[a].md`, and [intent B] reads `assets/[domain]/[b].md`.
561: Keep every path inside this skill folder and load a file only when it exists.
562: When two intents score close together, follow both in rank order.
563: When nothing matches, report `UNKNOWN_FALLBACK` with the checklist from the machine router instead of guessing.
564: The machine router lives in [`ROUTER.md`](./ROUTER.md); read it before selecting a resource.
565: 
566: ---
567: 
568: The link resolves to the sibling file, whose one heading the readers parse is:
569: 
570: \## MACHINE ROUTER
571: 
572: ```python
573: DEFAULT_RESOURCE = "references/[default].md"
574: INTENT_SIGNALS = {"PRIMARY": {"weight": 4, "keywords": [("[keyword]", 4), ("[phrase]", 3)]}}
575: RESOURCE_MAP = {"PRIMARY": ["references/[domain]/[primary].md"]}
576: UNKNOWN_FALLBACK_CHECKLIST = ["Confirm the routing key", "Confirm the intent", "Provide one concrete input"]
577: 
578: def route_[skill_name]_resources(user_request, task=None):
579:     inventory = discover_markdown_resources()
580:     primary, secondary, scores = classify_intents(user_request, task)
581:     if max(scores.values() or [0]) < 0.5:
582:         return {"load_level": "UNKNOWN_FALLBACK", "checklist": UNKNOWN_FALLBACK_CHECKLIST}
583:     return {"routing_key": get_routing_key(task, [primary]), "resources": inventory}
584: ```
585: 
586: The full resilience pattern (guarded paths, recursive discovery, routing keys) is in [skill-smart-router.md](./skill-smart-router.md).
587: 
588: **Writing Tips**:
589: - Open Section 2 with the signal that actually picks this skill's files.
590: - Name the first file to load, so a reader knows where to start.
591: - Name the router file with a markdown link, so a reader can open it.
592: - Keep `UNKNOWN_FALLBACK` as the named no-match outcome.
593: - Edit `INTENT_SIGNALS` and `RESOURCE_MAP` in `ROUTER.md` when the skill gains a domain.
594: - Avoid duplicate lookup tables, static file inventories, and unguarded `load()` calls.
595: 
596: **Word Budget**: 8-12 non-blank lines of prose
597: 
598: ---
599: 
600: ### Section 3: HOW IT WORKS
601: 
602: **Purpose**: Explain the skill's workflow, architecture, and key patterns
603: 
604: **Essential Content**:
605: - Process flow (visual diagram using ASCII)
606: - Key capabilities or components
607: - Configuration or setup requirements
608: - Examples of primary workflows
609: - Flowchart supplements for complex logic (NEW - when logic blocks present)
610: 
611: **Structure**:
612: 
613: ### [Primary Workflow Name]
614: 
615: [Brief explanation]
616: 
617: **Process Flow**:
618: \`\`\`
619: STEP 1: [Action]
620:    ├─ [Sub-task]
621:    └─ [Output]
622:    ↓
623: STEP 2: [Action]
624:    └─ [Output]
625: \`\`\`
626: 
627: **Example**:
628: \`\`\`[language]
629: # Realistic example
630: \`\`\`
631: 
632: **Writing Tips**:
633: - Use Mermaid for flow diagrams so a parser can read them.
634: - Show, don't just tell (include code examples)
635: - Progressive detail: Overview → specifics → edge cases
636: - Link to references for deep dives
637: - **Flowchart Supplements**: Add visual flowcharts before/after complex Python/YAML logic (see below)
638: 
639: **Word Budget**: 150-300 lines
640: 
641: ### Flowchart Supplements (For Complex Logic)
642: 
643: **Purpose**: Add visual clarity to complex Python/YAML logic blocks without removing structured code
644: 
645: **When to Use**:
646: - Complex conditional logic (nested if/else, multiple branches)
647: - Mode detection algorithms
648: - Multi-step decision trees
649: - Workflow routing logic
650: - State machine transitions
651: 
652: **Approach**:
653: - **Supplement, don't replace**: Keep existing Python/YAML code intact
654: - **Add flowcharts**: Place ASCII flowchart before or after code block
655: - **Visual aid purpose**: Help quick understanding of logic flow
656: 
657: **Structure**:
658: 
659: ### [Logic Section Name]
660: 
661: **[Brief explanation of what this logic does]**
662: 
663: **Logic Flow**:
664: \`\`\`
665: START
666:   ↓
667: [Check Condition A]
668:   ↓
669: A True? ─── NO ──→ [Path B]
670:   │                    ↓
671:   │              [Process B]
672:   │                    ↓
673:   YES              [Continue]
674:   ↓
675: [Process A]
676:   ↓
677: RESULT
678: \`\`\`
679: 
680: **Implementation**:
681: \`\`\`python
682: def example_logic(input):
683:     """Original Python logic preserved"""
684:     if condition_a:
685:         return process_a(input)
686:     else:
687:         return process_b(input)
688: \`\`\`
689: 
690: **OR for configuration:**
691: 
692: \`\`\`yaml
693: mode_detection:
694:   trigger_patterns:
695:     ticket: ["$ticket", "create ticket"]
696:     story: ["$story", "user story"]
697:   defaults:
698:     mode: interactive
699:     depth: 10
700: \`\`\`
701: 
702: **Writing Tips**:
703: - **Keep code**: Don't remove Python/YAML - it's precise and complete
704: - **Add diagrams**: Flowcharts provide at-a-glance understanding
705: - **Placement**:
706:   - Flowchart FIRST if it aids comprehension before reading code
707:   - Flowchart AFTER if it summarizes complex code
708:   - Both before AND after for very complex logic
709: - **Consistency**: Use the same ASCII flowchart style as the other diagrams in the file
710: - **When to skip**: Simple 2-3 line logic doesn't need flowcharts
711: 
712: **Example Use Cases**:
713: - Mode detection with 5+ conditions → Flowchart + Python code
714: - YAML configuration with complex triggers → Keep YAML, add decision tree diagram
715: - Multi-step workflow routing → Flowchart showing paths, keep implementation code
716: 
717: **Word Budget**: Variable (adds 10-30 lines per complex logic block)
718: 
719: ---
720: 
721: ### Section 4: RULES (REQUIRED)
722: 
723: **Purpose**: Define mandatory behaviors, prohibited actions, and escalation triggers
724: 
725: **Validation**: package_skill.py requires this section with specific subsections
726: 
727: **Essential Content** (all three subsections REQUIRED):
728: - ALWAYS rules (4-7 critical requirements)
729: - NEVER rules (3-5 anti-patterns to avoid)
730: - ESCALATE IF (3-5 situations requiring user input)
731: 
732: **Structure**:
733: 
734: ### ALWAYS
735: 
736: **ALWAYS do these without asking:**
737: 
738: 1. **ALWAYS [requirement]**
739:    - [Why this matters]
740:    - [Implementation detail]
741: 
742: ### NEVER
743: 
744: **NEVER do these:**
745: 
746: 1. **NEVER [anti-pattern]**
747:    - [Why problematic]
748:    - [Alternative approach]
749: 
750: ### ESCALATE IF
751: 
752: **Ask user when:**
753: 
754: 1. **ESCALATE IF [ambiguous situation]**
755:    - [What's unclear]
756:    - [What clarification needed]
757: 
758: **Writing Tips**:
759: - Use ALL CAPS for subsection headers: `ALWAYS`, `NEVER`, `ESCALATE IF` (or `ESCALATE WHEN`)
760: - Be specific and actionable
761: - Explain *why* for each rule (rationale matters)
762: - Include implementation guidance
763: - Present options to user for ESCALATE IF cases
764: 
765: **Word Budget**: 100-200 lines
766: 
767: ---
768: 
769: ### Section 5: REFERENCES
770: 
771: **Purpose**: Expose the operational references and templates the skill depends on.
772: 
773: **Essential Content**:
774: - Core references used during execution
775: - Templates/assets used during output generation
776: - Loading notes that stay consistent with Section 2 (SMART ROUTING)
777: 
778: **Structure**:
779: 
780: ### Core References
781: - [reference-name.md](./references/reference-name.md) - Primary guidance
782: 
783: ### Templates and Assets
784: - [template-name.md](./assets/template-name.md) - Reusable output template

786: ### Reference Loading Notes
787: - Load only what current intent requires.

795: 
796: **Purpose**: Define completion conditions and quality standards

799: - Completion checklist (5-10 items)

815: **Before marking complete:**
816: 
817: - **[Dimension]**: [Specific requirement]

819:

821: - Use checkbox format `- [ ]` for checklists
822: - Specific and measurable criteria
823: - Include both completion and quality checks
824: - Define thresholds numerically where possible

831: 
832: **Purpose**: Document how skill integrates with systems, tools, and workflow contracts
833: 
834: **Essential Content**:
835: - Validation workflow integration
836: - Required workflow contracts and handoff rules
837: - Tool usage patterns
838: - Knowledge base dependencies
839: - External tool requirements

842:

862: ### External Tools
863: 
864: **[Tool Name]**:
865: - Installation: [How]

868: **Writing Tips**:
869: - Distinguish required vs. optional dependencies
870: - Provide installation/setup instructions for external tools
871: - Explain fallback behavior if optional resources missing
872: - Link related skills by name
873: 
874: **Word Budget**: 50-150 lines

878: ## 5. COMMON PITFALLS
879: 
880: For the complete list of 8 common pitfalls with before/after examples, see:
881: → **[common-pitfalls.md](../../references/shared/common-pitfalls.md)**

883: **Quick Summary:**
884: 1. Generic descriptions → Be specific about capabilities
885: 2. Bloated SKILL.md → Move details to references/
886: 3. Missing bundled resources → Identify repeated code/docs
887: 4. Unclear triggers → Specific activation conditions
888: 5. Distant instructions → Use the [Prose Clarity Checklist](../../references/skill/creation-workflow.md#prose-clarity-checklist)
889: 6. Platform-specific claims → Stay platform-agnostic
890: 7. Multiline YAML descriptions → Keep single line

899: ## 6. QUALITY CHECKLIST & QUICK REFERENCE
900: 
901: ### Pre-Packaging Checklist
902: 
903: **Before running package_skill.py:**
904: 
905: Frontmatter:
906: □ YAML frontmatter present and valid

909: □ Description uses third-person voice

911: □ No angle brackets in description

931: □ No duplication between SKILL.md and references/

934: □ Section 1 (WHEN TO USE) contains ONLY activation triggers and use cases
935: □ Section 1 does NOT contain file-path routing logic
936: □ SMART ROUTING section exists (Section 2 - REQUIRED for all skills)
937: □ Section 2 is 8-12 non-blank lines of plain prose: what selects this skill, what it loads first, where the machine router is

943: □ Flowchart supplements added to complex logic blocks in Section 3 (where applicable)

961: | --------------------- | -------------------------- | -------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |

14: # SKILL.md File Templates - Creation Guide
15: 
16: Templates for creating SKILL.md files with proper structure, frontmatter, and required sections.
17: 
18: ---
19: 
20: ## 1. OVERVIEW
21: 
22: ### Purpose of SKILL.md Files
23: 
24: SKILL.md files define AI agent skills - reusable capabilities that extend an agent's functionality for specific domains or workflows. A well-crafted SKILL.md:
25: 
26: - **Triggers automatically** when relevant patterns are detected
27: - **Guides the agent** through specialized workflows
28: - **Maintains consistency** across conversations
29: - **Encodes expertise** in specific domains
30: 
31: ### Template Overview
32: 
33: This guide provides **one comprehensive SKILL template** (Section 3) that covers all skill types from simple single-purpose tools to complex multi-mode orchestrators.
34: 
35: **The template is flexible:**
36: - **Simple skills**: Use required core sections only (WHEN TO USE, SMART ROUTING, HOW IT WORKS, RULES, REFERENCES)
37: - **Skills with bundled resources**: Say in Section 2 what selects the skill and what it loads first, and put the router in the sibling `ROUTER.md`. Use `references/`, `assets/`, and `scripts/`
38: - **Multi-mode skills**: Expand WHEN TO USE and HOW IT WORKS sections by mode
39: - **All skills**: Section 2 (SMART ROUTING) is required: 8 to 12 non-blank lines of plain prose
40: 
41: **Target size**: 800-2000 lines for SKILL.md (<5k words total)
42: 
43: **Examples**:
44: - Simple: Unit test generator, documentation formatter (no bundled resources)
45: - Moderate: API client, specialized code reviewer (with references and assets)
46: - Complex: Workflow orchestrator, document quality pipeline (multi-mode with extensive resources)
47: 
48: ### Progressive Disclosure Principle
49: 
50: SKILL.md architecture follows progressive disclosure:
51: 
52: 1. **Metadata** (YAML frontmatter) - Always in context (~100 words)
53: 2. **SKILL.md body** - When skill activates (<5k words)
54: 3. **Bundled resources** - Loaded as needed (unlimited size)
55: 
56: **Critical**: Keep SKILL.md <5k words. Move detailed content to `references/`, `scripts/`, or `assets/`.
57: 
58: ### Document Type Requirements
59: 
60: **Enforcement Level**: STRICT (SKILL.md files require perfect structure)
61: 
62: **Required Elements**:
63: - ✅ YAML frontmatter with required fields
64: - ✅ H1 title with subtitle
65: - ✅ Numbered H2 sections (ALL CAPS, integers only, never a letter suffix such as `2b.`)
66: - ✅ Section separators (`---`)
67: - ✅ No table of contents (forbidden in SKILL.md)
68: 
69: **Quality Targets**:
70: - Structure: 100/100
71: - Content quality: High (AI-evaluated)
72: - Overall: High (human/AI judgment)
73: 
74: ---
75: 
76: ## 2. FRONTMATTER REQUIREMENTS
77: 
78: ### Required Fields
79: 
80: | Field | Required | Format | Example |
81: |-------|----------|--------|---------|
82: | `name` | ✅ | hyphen-case | `my-skill-name` |
83: | `description` | ✅ | Single line, **≤ 130 chars** for skills (≤ 110 for commands), 1,536-char hard cap | `"Handles X when Y occurs"` |
84: | `allowed-tools` | ✅ | Array: `[Tool1, Tool2]` | `[Read, Write, Edit, Bash]` |
85: | `version` | ✅ | 4-part X.Y.Z.W | `1.0.0.0` |
86: 
87: > **Hard rules**: not a frontmatter key. They live in `hard-rules.json` beside the skill's `SKILL.md`, a JSON array of `{id, check, message, severity}` objects that the dispatch preflight reads.
88: 
89: > **Description budget & trim style**: see [`frontmatter-templates.md` § Description Budget & Trim Style](../../../sk-create-frontmatter/assets/frontmatter-templates.md).
90: > Keep total project descriptions under the ~6,400-character ceiling. This leaves headroom below the 8,000-character auto-discovery limit.
91: > Drop product and stack lists. Drop marketing prose. Keep the skill name, primary verb, domain noun and mode suffixes (`:auto` or `:confirm`).
92: 
93: ### Template
94: 
95: ```yaml
96: ---
97: name: sk-example
98: description: Example workflow skill demonstrating proper frontmatter format with specific capabilities, use cases, and key differentiators for AI agent discovery.
99: allowed-tools: [Read, Write, Edit, Bash, Glob, Grep]
100: version: 1.0.0.0
101: ---
102: ```
103: 
104: ### Key Rules
105: 
106: - **name**: Must match folder name exactly, hyphen-case only
107: - **description**: Third-person voice, single line, no `<>` brackets
108: - **allowed-tools**: Use brackets `[...]`, not comma-separated string

423: ```

426: └── Bundled Resources

429:     └── assets/           - Templates and examples (subfolders OK)

435: - **references/** = flat for small skills, domain subfolders for medium/complex skills
436:   - Flat example: `references/core-standards.md`, `references/validation.md`
437:   - Domain example: `references/backend/go/`, `references/frontend/react/`
438: - **assets/** = Subfolders ALLOWED when organizing many files by category

440:   - Example: `assets/skill/`, `assets/readme/`, `assets/flowcharts/`
441: - **scripts/** = Typically flat, but subfolders OK for large script collections

444: - Skills auto-discovered from `.skilled/skills/*/SKILL.md` frontmatter
445: - Skill name in frontmatter MUST match folder name

503: 
504: ### Section 2: SMART ROUTING (Required for All Skills)
505: 
506: **Purpose**: Use this section to explain how you route a request to this skill's resources.
507: 
508: **Three skill kinds, one shape**:
509: 
510: | Kind | How to tell | What Section 2 says |
511: |------|-------------|---------------------|
512: | Hub | the folder holds `mode-registry.json` and `hub-router.json` | how a prompt reaches a mode, and where the root `ROUTER.md` is |
513: | Mode packet | a packet folder inside a hub | what selects this packet, what it loads first, and where its own `ROUTER.md` is |
514: | Standalone | neither hub file | the same as a mode packet, with the router in its own `ROUTER.md` |
515: 
516: **The limit**: 12 non-blank lines and 180 words are the hard ceilings the check enforces. Aim for 8 to 12 lines. A packet or standalone skill says three things: what selects it, what it loads first, and where the machine router is.
517: 
518: **The sibling router**: the machine router lives in `ROUTER.md` beside `SKILL.md`, under a final `## MACHINE ROUTER` heading.
519: That heading is the one every reader parses. Its section number is optional, so `## MACHINE ROUTER` and `## 9. MACHINE ROUTER` both count, and the check ignores the number.
520: Keep pseudocode out of SMART ROUTING and put it in that section.
521: `SKILL.md` carries no `## MACHINE ROUTER` section of its own: two homes for one router is the dual declaration the check reports.
522: 
523: **The link line**: Section 2 names the router file with a relative markdown link, [`ROUTER.md`](./ROUTER.md), and its target resolves on disk. A sentence that mentions the name without a link fails, because a reader cannot follow it to a file that is not there.
524: 
525: **One router per folder**: every skill and every mode packet owns `ROUTER.md` inside its own folder, linked from its own `SKILL.md`. A router file whose real path leaves the folder is not that skill's router.
526: 
527: **The no-match outcome** is named `UNKNOWN_FALLBACK` everywhere. Low confidence returns a disambiguation checklist, never an empty result and never a guess.
528: 
529: **Validation**: `package_skill.py --strict` reports the routing shape with five codes:
530: 
531: | Code | Finding |
532: |------|---------|
533: | `RS-001` | SMART ROUTING is longer than the limit (12 lines or 180 words by default) |
534: | `RS-002` | `SKILL.md` carries a `## MACHINE ROUTER` section, with or without a code block |
535: | `RS-003` | A `## MACHINE ROUTER` section is not the last H2 of the document that holds it |
536: | `RS-004` | the skill has no sibling `ROUTER.md`, or its real path leaves the skill folder |
537: | `RS-005` | `SKILL.md` has no relative markdown link to `./ROUTER.md` that resolves |
538: 
539: The machine block itself is a fenced block or an unfenced run of indented lines.
540: It declares the router with one of these markers: `INTENT_SIGNALS =`, `RESOURCE_MAP =`, `DEFAULT_RESOURCE =`, `UNKNOWN_FALLBACK_CHECKLIST =`, `def discover_markdown_resources` or `def _guard_in_skill`.
541: A fence closes only on a run of the same character that is at least as long as its opening run.
542: 
543: **Known debt** is listed in `sk-create-skill/scripts/routing-shape-known-debt.json`.
544: Entries use skill paths relative to `.skilled/skills`, such as `sk-code/sk-code-review`.
545: A folder outside that root is never debt.
546: Each entry records `{"lines", "words", "machineBlocks", "codes"}`.
547: A listed skill fails if its line count, word count or machine blocks left in `SKILL.md` exceed the record, or if it adds an unrecorded code.
548: The checker ignores entries in any other form.
549: Remove an entry when the skill follows the canon.
550: 
551: **Placement**: the SMART ROUTING section sits after Section 1 (WHEN TO USE) and before HOW IT WORKS, and `ROUTER.md` sits beside `SKILL.md` at the skill root.
552: 
553: **Worked example** (a canon Section 2 and its sibling router, nothing else):
554: 
555: \## 2. SMART ROUTING
556: 
557: Use this skill for [domain] work: [trigger 1], [trigger 2], or [trigger 3].
558: The first signal is [project/stack/mode detection], because it picks the knowledge folder before any intent scoring.
559: Load `references/[default].md` first on every run. The other files assume it.
560: Then load what the matched intent maps to: [intent A] reads `references/[domain]/[a].md`, and [intent B] reads `assets/[domain]/[b].md`.
561: Keep every path inside this skill folder and load a file only when it exists.
562: When two intents score close together, follow both in rank order.
563: When nothing matches, report `UNKNOWN_FALLBACK` with the checklist from the machine router instead of guessing.
564: The machine router lives in [`ROUTER.md`](./ROUTER.md); read it before selecting a resource.
565: 
566: ---
567: 
568: The link resolves to the sibling file, whose one heading the readers parse is:
569: 
570: \## MACHINE ROUTER
571: 
572: ```python
573: DEFAULT_RESOURCE = "references/[default].md"
574: INTENT_SIGNALS = {"PRIMARY": {"weight": 4, "keywords": [("[keyword]", 4), ("[phrase]", 3)]}}
575: RESOURCE_MAP = {"PRIMARY": ["references/[domain]/[primary].md"]}
576: UNKNOWN_FALLBACK_CHECKLIST = ["Confirm the routing key", "Confirm the intent", "Provide one concrete input"]
577: 
578: def route_[skill_name]_resources(user_request, task=None):
579:     inventory = discover_markdown_resources()
580:     primary, secondary, scores = classify_intents(user_request, task)
581:     if max(scores.values() or [0]) < 0.5:
582:         return {"load_level": "UNKNOWN_FALLBACK", "checklist": UNKNOWN_FALLBACK_CHECKLIST}
583:     return {"routing_key": get_routing_key(task, [primary]), "resources": inventory}
584: ```
585: 
586: The full resilience pattern (guarded paths, recursive discovery, routing keys) is in [skill-smart-router.md](./skill-smart-router.md).
587: 
588: **Writing Tips**:
589: - Open Section 2 with the signal that actually picks this skill's files.
590: - Name the first file to load, so a reader knows where to start.
591: - Name the router file with a markdown link, so a reader can open it.
592: - Keep `UNKNOWN_FALLBACK` as the named no-match outcome.
593: - Edit `INTENT_SIGNALS` and `RESOURCE_MAP` in `ROUTER.md` when the skill gains a domain.
594: - Avoid duplicate lookup tables, static file inventories, and unguarded `load()` calls.
595: 
596: **Word Budget**: 8-12 non-blank lines of prose

14: # Skill Procedure Card Templates - Creation Guidelines
15: 
16: Templates and guidelines for creating private procedure cards: repeatable, selectable processes bundled inside a skill or mode without becoming a new public identity.
17: 
18: ## 1. OVERVIEW
19: 
20: ### What Is a Procedure Card
21: 
22: A procedure card is a private markdown file that adds a repeatable, triggerable PROCESS to an existing skill or mode. It is not a public skill, not a public mode, and does not appear in any advisor routing table. A skill or hub always resolves its public identity first (through its own routing, or a parent hub's `mode-registry.json`). A procedure card is only ever selected AFTER that, from inside the already-chosen skill or mode, by matching the card's own `Trigger` field against the request. A card never grants tool permissions beyond what the owning skill or mode already has.
23: 
24: ### Location & Naming
25: 
26: **Standalone skill**: `references/procedures/[procedure-name].md`
27: 
28: **Parent hub, packet-local**: `[packet-name]/procedures/[procedure-name].md`
29: 
30: **Parent hub, cross-packet shared**: `shared/procedures/[procedure-name].md`, only when the procedure genuinely coordinates two or more packets and cannot be owned by one packet without duplicating orchestration.
31: 
32: **Naming Convention**: kebab-case with `.md` extension, same rule as `references/` and `assets/`.
33: 
34: | ✅ Valid Names | ❌ Invalid Names |
35: |---------------|-----------------|
36: | `sensitive-field-redaction.md` | `SensitiveFieldRedaction.md` (PascalCase) |
37: | `digital-signature-verification.md` | `digital_signature_verification.md` (snake_case) |
38: | `batch-annotation-cleanup.md` | `batchAnnotationCleanup.MD` (wrong case) |
39: 
40: ### When to Create a Procedure Card
41: 
42: **Create a procedure card when:**
43: - The skill or mode has multiple distinct, individually-triggered internal procedures, not one dominant workflow.
44: - Each procedure needs a strict, lint-able, consistent shape (required fields in a fixed order), not free-form prose.
45: - Fine-grained behavior selection matters, but creating N public skills or modes for what is really one skill or mode with N internal procedures would over-fragment the public surface.
46: - `SKILL.md`'s `HOW IT WORKS` section would otherwise balloon into several near-duplicate workflow write-ups.
47: 
48: **Keep it a plain reference (`skill-reference-template.md`) instead when:**
49: - There is only one dominant workflow, so no selection step is needed.
50: - The content is general background knowledge or context, not an actionable process with its own trigger.
51: - The content always applies whenever the skill or mode runs, rather than only on a specific request shape.
52: 
53: ---
54: 
55: ## 2. DOCUMENT STRUCTURE
56: 
57: ### Title and Intro
58: 
59: **CRITICAL: The intro after the H1 title must be 1-2 SHORT sentences only.**
60: 
61: ```markdown
62: ---
63: title: [Card Title]
64: description: One-line summary of the card's behavior.
65: trigger_phrases:
66:   - "[primary card trigger]"
67:   - "[alternate request phrasing]"
68: importance_tier: normal
69: contextType: implementation
70: version: 1.0.0.0
71: ---
72: 
73: # [Card Title]
74: 
75: [1-2 SHORT sentences: what process this card adds and to which skill or mode.]
76: 
77: ## 1. REQUIRED FIELDS
78: 
79: [table, see Section 3]
80: 
81: ## N. PROCEDURE
82: 
83: [numbered operating steps]
84: ```
85: 
86: Every card carries the same full 5-field frontmatter block used by references and assets: `title`, `description`, 3-8 lowercase multi-word `trigger_phrases`, `importance_tier` (`normal` unless the card is a formal cross-packet contract), `contextType` (`implementation` for nearly all procedure cards), plus `version`. See [frontmatter-templates.md](../../../sk-create-frontmatter/assets/frontmatter-templates.md) for field rules.
87: 
88: ### Body Order
89: 
90: Every card follows this fixed order:
91: 
92: 1. H1 title matching `title`.
93: 2. One-sentence intro.
94: 3. `## 1. REQUIRED FIELDS`, the seven fields below, in order, non-empty.
95: 4. Optional numbered sections (placement rationale, related cards, conflict rule, read-only compatibility, tool boundary) only when applicable.
96: 5. Numbered `## N. PROCEDURE`, the operating steps.
97: 
98: ---
99: 
100: ## 3. REQUIRED FIELDS
101: 
102: Every procedure card uses these seven fields in this order:
103: 
104: | Field | Requirement |
105: |---|---|
106: | Purpose | One sentence describing the behavior the card adds to the owning skill or mode. |
107: | Owning skill/mode | The standalone skill, or the parent-hub packet, that owns this card, or `shared` with an explicit owning reviewer for a card that coordinates multiple packets. |
108: | Source reference | External source filename only, if the card adapts an external skill, prompt, or spec, or `No external source` with rationale. Never paste source prose into the card. |
109: | Trigger | Concrete request patterns or conditions that make the card applicable, evaluated only after the public skill or mode has already been selected. |
110: | Output contract | The exact artifact, report, or handoff the procedure must produce. |
111: | Proof gate | The evidence required before the card can be considered followed. |
112: | Privacy rule | A statement that the card is private implementation guidance and does not create a public skill, command, or mode. |
113: 
114: ---
115: 
116: ## 4. OPTIONAL FIELDS
117: 
118: Use these only when they materially improve reviewability:
119: 
120: | Field | Use |
121: |---|---|
122: | Placement rationale | Required for any `shared/procedures/` card, optional for a packet-local card. |
123: | Related cards | Names of cards that may be loaded before or after this one. |
124: | Conflict rule | How to choose between overlapping cards inside the same skill or mode. |
125: | Read-only compatibility | Required when the owning skill or mode is read-only. States that the card may be cited to produce guidance or a handoff without writing files or running commands. |
126: | Tool boundary | Required when the owning skill or mode can mutate the workspace. States the mutating permission boundary and that the card does not widen it. |
127: 
128: ---
129: 
130: ## 5. COMPLETE WORKED EXAMPLE
131: 
132: ```markdown
133: ---
134: title: Sensitive-Field Redaction Pass
135: description: Private procedure card for the pdf-editor skill's redaction workflow across form fields, embedded metadata, and annotations.
136: trigger_phrases:
137:   - "redact sensitive fields"
138:   - "pdf redaction pass"
139:   - "remove pii from pdf"
140: importance_tier: normal
141: contextType: implementation
142: version: 1.0.0.0
143: ---
144: 
145: # Sensitive-Field Redaction Pass
146: 
147: Private procedure card for applying the pdf-editor skill's redaction workflow.
148: 
149: ## 1. REQUIRED FIELDS
150: 
151: | Field | Value |
152: |---|---|
153: | Purpose | Let `pdf-editor` remove sensitive form-field values, embedded metadata, and annotation text before a document is shared externally. |
154: | Owning skill/mode | `pdf-editor` |
155: | Source reference | No external source |
156: | Trigger | Use when the request asks to redact, sanitize, or remove PII or sensitive content from a PDF before sharing. |
157: | Output contract | A redacted PDF with confirmed-empty form fields, stripped metadata, and a redaction log listing every field and annotation touched. |
158: | Proof gate | The redaction log accounts for every form field and annotation in the source document, and none are silently skipped. |
159: | Privacy rule | This is private redaction guidance and not a public redaction skill. |
160: 
161: ## 2. TOOL BOUNDARY
162: 
163: `pdf-editor` may write the redacted output file. This card does not grant any permission beyond the skill's existing Write access to its own output directory.
164: 
165: ## 3. PROCEDURE
166: 
167: 1. Enumerate every form field, metadata key, and annotation in the source PDF before touching any of them.
168: 2. Classify each as sensitive or not, using the request's stated redaction scope.
169: 3. Clear sensitive form-field values and strip sensitive metadata keys, and leave non-sensitive content untouched.
170: 4. Remove or blank sensitive annotation text.
171: 5. Write the redacted output and a redaction log naming every field, key, and annotation that was cleared.
172: 6. Confirm the log's field count matches the enumeration from step 1, with no silent skips.
173: ```
174: 
175: This example is deliberately self-contained: see [examples-and-maintenance.md](../../references/skill/examples-and-maintenance.md) for how it extends the PDF Editor skill layout into a multi-procedure shape.
176: 
177: ---
178: 
179: ## 6. SELECTION RULES
180: 
181: 1. The public skill or mode is resolved first, through the skill's own routing or a parent hub's `mode-registry.json`. A procedure card never changes that resolution.
182: 2. The selected skill or mode evaluates only its own `procedures/` folder, plus (parent hubs only) shared cards under `shared/procedures/` whose trigger names it.
183: 3. A skill/mode-local exact trigger beats a shared card.
184: 4. When two local cards match, choose the card with the narrower output contract.
185: 5. If no card matches, the skill or mode follows its existing `SKILL.md` behavior and states that no procedure card applied.
186: 6. (Parent hubs only) If a request spans multiple packets, the hub still decides the bundle, and cards never change public routing.
187: 
188: ---
189: 
190: ## 7. SOURCE ADAPTATION RULES
191: 
192: Use these when a card adapts an external skill, prompt, or spec into OpenCode-native process:
193: 
194: 1. Cite only the external source's filename.
195: 2. Preserve intent, not phrasing.
196: 3. Rewrite the procedure steps in the owning skill or mode's own tool boundary and vocabulary.
197: 4. Do not include long source excerpts, starter code, command snippets, or proprietary prompt text.
198: 5. Review the card by comparing purpose, trigger, output contract, and proof gate against the source's theme, not by diffing prose.
199: 
200: ---
201: 
202: ## 8. PROCEDURE CARD CHECKLIST
203: 
204: **Before publishing or updating a card, verify:**
205: 
206: ```markdown
207: Structure:
208: □ Frontmatter includes title, description, trigger_phrases, importance_tier, contextType, and version.
209: □ H1 title matches the card title, and the intro is 1-2 sentences with no subsections.
210: □ Required fields appear in the required order with non-empty values.
211: □ Optional sections and the PROCEDURE section are numbered sequentially.
212: 
213: Content:
214: □ Source reference uses filename-only citation, or "No external source" with rationale.
215: □ Output contract and proof gate are concrete enough to grade pass/fail.
216: □ A read-only owning skill/mode does not gain Write, Edit, Bash, or execution authority through the card.
217: 
218: Placement:
219: □ Card lives under references/procedures/, <packet>/procedures/, or shared/procedures/ per Section 1.
220: □ Shared cards name an owning reviewer and a placement rationale.
221: □ Related cards and conflict rules (if present) point to real neighboring cards.
222: ```
223: 
224: ---
225: 
226: ## 9. REFERENCES AND RELATED RESOURCES
227: 
228: ### Real-World Implementation
229: 
230: `sk-design` (`.skilled/skills/sk-design/`) is an illustrative hub-scale example: its current registry has two workflow modes and one transport packet, with procedure cards owned by the workflow packets plus shared coordination cards. Consult `sk-design/mode-registry.json` before copying this topology. `sk-design/shared/procedure-card-schema.md` is the schema this template generalizes from.
231: 
232: ### Templates
233: - [skill-reference-template.md](./skill-reference-template.md) - Reference file templates (use when no trigger-based selection is needed)
234: - [skill-asset-template.md](./skill-asset-template.md) - Asset file templates
235: - [frontmatter-templates.md](../../../sk-create-frontmatter/assets/frontmatter-templates.md) - Frontmatter by document type
236: 
237: ### Standards
238: - [core-standards.md](../../../shared/references/core-standards.md) - Document type rules

28: **Parent hub, packet-local**: `[packet-name]/procedures/[procedure-name].md`
29: 
30: **Parent hub, cross-packet shared**: `shared/procedures/[procedure-name].md`, only when the procedure genuinely coordinates two or more packets and cannot be owned by one packet without duplicating orchestration.
31: 
32: **Naming Convention**: kebab-case with `.md` extension, same rule as `references/` and `assets/`.
33: 
34: | ✅ Valid Names | ❌ Invalid Names |
35: |---------------|-----------------|
36: | `sensitive-field-redaction.md` | `SensitiveFieldRedaction.md` (PascalCase) |
37: | `digital-signature-verification.md` | `digital_signature_verification.md` (snake_case) |
38: | `batch-annotation-cleanup.md` | `batchAnnotationCleanup.MD` (wrong case) |
39: 
40: ### When to Create a Procedure Card
41: 
42: **Create a procedure card when:**
43: - The skill or mode has multiple distinct, individually-triggered internal procedures, not one dominant workflow.
44: - Each procedure needs a strict, lint-able, consistent shape (required fields in a fixed order), not free-form prose.
45: - Fine-grained behavior selection matters, but creating N public skills or modes for what is really one skill or mode with N internal procedures would over-fragment the public surface.
46: - `SKILL.md`'s `HOW IT WORKS` section would otherwise balloon into several near-duplicate workflow write-ups.
47: 
48: **Keep it a plain reference (`skill-reference-template.md`) instead when:**
49: - There is only one dominant workflow, so no selection step is needed.
50: - The content is general background knowledge or context, not an actionable process with its own trigger.
51: - The content always applies whenever the skill or mode runs, rather than only on a specific request shape.
52: 
53: ---
54: 
55: ## 2. DOCUMENT STRUCTURE
56: 
57: ### Title and Intro
58: 
59: **CRITICAL: The intro after the H1 title must be 1-2 SHORT sentences only.**
60: 
61: ```markdown
62: ---
63: title: [Card Title]
64: description: One-line summary of the card's behavior.
65: trigger_phrases:
66:   - "[primary card trigger]"
67:   - "[alternate request phrasing]"
68: importance_tier: normal
69: contextType: implementation
70: version: 1.0.0.0
71: ---
72: 
73: # [Card Title]
74: 
75: [1-2 SHORT sentences: what process this card adds and to which skill or mode.]
76: 
77: ## 1. REQUIRED FIELDS
78: 
79: [table, see Section 3]
80: 
81: ## N. PROCEDURE
82: 
83: [numbered operating steps]
84: ```
85: 
86: Every card carries the same full 5-field frontmatter block used by references and assets: `title`, `description`, 3-8 lowercase multi-word `trigger_phrases`, `importance_tier` (`normal` unless the card is a formal cross-packet contract), `contextType` (`implementation` for nearly all procedure cards), plus `version`. See [frontmatter-templates.md](../../../sk-create-frontmatter/assets/frontmatter-templates.md) for field rules.
87: 
88: ### Body Order
89: 
90: Every card follows this fixed order:
91: 
92: 1. H1 title matching `title`.
93: 2. One-sentence intro.
94: 3. `## 1. REQUIRED FIELDS`, the seven fields below, in order, non-empty.
95: 4. Optional numbered sections (placement rationale, related cards, conflict rule, read-only compatibility, tool boundary) only when applicable.
96: 5. Numbered `## N. PROCEDURE`, the operating steps.
97: 
98: ---
99: 
100: ## 3. REQUIRED FIELDS
101: 
102: Every procedure card uses these seven fields in this order:
103: 
104: | Field | Requirement |
105: |---|---|
106: | Purpose | One sentence describing the behavior the card adds to the owning skill or mode. |
107: | Owning skill/mode | The standalone skill, or the parent-hub packet, that owns this card, or `shared` with an explicit owning reviewer for a card that coordinates multiple packets. |
108: | Source reference | External source filename only, if the card adapts an external skill, prompt, or spec, or `No external source` with rationale. Never paste source prose into the card. |
109: | Trigger | Concrete request patterns or conditions that make the card applicable, evaluated only after the public skill or mode has already been selected. |
110: | Output contract | The exact artifact, report, or handoff the procedure must produce. |
111: | Proof gate | The evidence required before the card can be considered followed. |
112: | Privacy rule | A statement that the card is private implementation guidance and does not create a public skill, command, or mode. |
113: 
114: ---
115: 
116: ## 4. OPTIONAL FIELDS
117: 
118: Use these only when they materially improve reviewability:
119: 
120: | Field | Use |
121: |---|---|
122: | Placement rationale | Required for any `shared/procedures/` card, optional for a packet-local card. |
123: | Related cards | Names of cards that may be loaded before or after this one. |
124: | Conflict rule | How to choose between overlapping cards inside the same skill or mode. |
125: | Read-only compatibility | Required when the owning skill or mode is read-only. States that the card may be cited to produce guidance or a handoff without writing files or running commands. |
126: | Tool boundary | Required when the owning skill or mode can mutate the workspace. States the mutating permission boundary and that the card does not widen it. |
127: 
128: ---
129: 
130: ## 5. COMPLETE WORKED EXAMPLE
131: 
132: ```markdown
133: ---
134: title: Sensitive-Field Redaction Pass
135: description: Private procedure card for the pdf-editor skill's redaction workflow across form fields, embedded metadata, and annotations.
136: trigger_phrases:
137:   - "redact sensitive fields"
138:   - "pdf redaction pass"
139:   - "remove pii from pdf"
140: importance_tier: normal
141: contextType: implementation
142: version: 1.0.0.0
143: ---
144: 
145: # Sensitive-Field Redaction Pass
146: 
147: Private procedure card for applying the pdf-editor skill's redaction workflow.
148: 
149: ## 1. REQUIRED FIELDS
150: 
151: | Field | Value |
152: |---|---|
153: | Purpose | Let `pdf-editor` remove sensitive form-field values, embedded metadata, and annotation text before a document is shared externally. |
154: | Owning skill/mode | `pdf-editor` |
155: | Source reference | No external source |
156: | Trigger | Use when the request asks to redact, sanitize, or remove PII or sensitive content from a PDF before sharing. |
157: | Output contract | A redacted PDF with confirmed-empty form fields, stripped metadata, and a redaction log listing every field and annotation touched. |
158: | Proof gate | The redaction log accounts for every form field and annotation in the source document, and none are silently skipped. |
159: | Privacy rule | This is private redaction guidance and not a public redaction skill. |
160: 
161: ## 2. TOOL BOUNDARY
162: 
163: `pdf-editor` may write the redacted output file. This card does not grant any permission beyond the skill's existing Write access to its own output directory.
164: 
165: ## 3. PROCEDURE
166: 
167: 1. Enumerate every form field, metadata key, and annotation in the source PDF before touching any of them.
168: 2. Classify each as sensitive or not, using the request's stated redaction scope.
169: 3. Clear sensitive form-field values and strip sensitive metadata keys, and leave non-sensitive content untouched.
170: 4. Remove or blank sensitive annotation text.
171: 5. Write the redacted output and a redaction log naming every field, key, and annotation that was cleared.
172: 6. Confirm the log's field count matches the enumeration from step 1, with no silent skips.
173: ```
174: 
175: This example is deliberately self-contained: see [examples-and-maintenance.md](../../references/skill/examples-and-maintenance.md) for how it extends the PDF Editor skill layout into a multi-procedure shape.
176: 
177: ---
178: 
179: ## 6. SELECTION RULES
180: 
181: 1. The public skill or mode is resolved first, through the skill's own routing or a parent hub's `mode-registry.json`. A procedure card never changes that resolution.
182: 2. The selected skill or mode evaluates only its own `procedures/` folder, plus (parent hubs only) shared cards under `shared/procedures/` whose trigger names it.
183: 3. A skill/mode-local exact trigger beats a shared card.
184: 4. When two local cards match, choose the card with the narrower output contract.
185: 5. If no card matches, the skill or mode follows its existing `SKILL.md` behavior and states that no procedure card applied.
186: 6. (Parent hubs only) If a request spans multiple packets, the hub still decides the bundle, and cards never change public routing.
187: 
188: ---
189: 
190: ## 7. SOURCE ADAPTATION RULES
191: 
192: Use these when a card adapts an external skill, prompt, or spec into OpenCode-native process:
193: 
194: 1. Cite only the external source's filename.
195: 2. Preserve intent, not phrasing.
196: 3. Rewrite the procedure steps in the owning skill or mode's own tool boundary and vocabulary.
197: 4. Do not include long source excerpts, starter code, command snippets, or proprietary prompt text.
198: 5. Review the card by comparing purpose, trigger, output contract, and proof gate against the source's theme, not by diffing prose.
199: 
200: ---
201: 
202: ## 8. PROCEDURE CARD CHECKLIST
203: 
204: **Before publishing or updating a card, verify:**
205: 
206: ```markdown
207: Structure:
208: □ Frontmatter includes title, description, trigger_phrases, importance_tier, contextType, and version.
209: □ H1 title matches the card title, and the intro is 1-2 sentences with no subsections.
210: □ Required fields appear in the required order with non-empty values.
211: □ Optional sections and the PROCEDURE section are numbered sequentially.
212: 
213: Content:
214: □ Source reference uses filename-only citation, or "No external source" with rationale.
215: □ Output contract and proof gate are concrete enough to grade pass/fail.
216: □ A read-only owning skill/mode does not gain Write, Edit, Bash, or execution authority through the card.
217: 
218: Placement:
219: □ Card lives under references/procedures/, <packet>/procedures/, or shared/procedures/ per Section 1.
220: □ Shared cards name an owning reviewer and a placement rationale.
221: □ Related cards and conflict rules (if present) point to real neighboring cards.
222: ```
223: 
224: ---
225: 
226: ## 9. REFERENCES AND RELATED RESOURCES

Consult `sk-design/mode-registry.json` before copying this topology. `sk-design/shared/procedure-card-schema.md` is the schema this template generalizes from.

305: ## 5. LOGIC REPRESENTATION PATTERNS
306: 
307: **Purpose**: Guidelines for representing logic, workflows, and decision trees in asset files using structured formats instead of prose.
308: 
309: **Why Structured Logic?**
310: - **Clarity**: Executable-style logic is easier to understand than prose
311: - **AI-Friendly**: LLMs parse structured logic better than narrative descriptions
312: - **Maintainability**: Changes to logic are more visible in structured formats
313: - **Consistency**: Same patterns across all asset files
314: 
315: ### When to Use Each Format
316: 
317: **Use Python Pseudo-Code When:**
318: - Complex branching logic (multiple IF/ELIF/ELSE conditions)
319: - Function/method definitions with clear inputs/outputs
320: - State management or algorithmic processes
321: - Validation or transformation logic
322: - Examples: Mode detection, validation pipelines, decision functions
323: 
324: **Use YAML Structures When:**
325: - Configuration data (settings, options, parameters)
326: - Pipeline definitions (multi-step workflows with clear phases)
327: - Hierarchical workflows (nested processes)
328: - Metadata structures (categorization, tagging)
329: - Examples: Workflow definitions, configuration templates, feature matrices
330: 
331: **Use Markdown Decision Trees When:**
332: - Simple branching logic (2-5 branches)
333: - Visual flow representation (user-facing paths)
334: - Classification systems (type determination)
335: - Quick decision guides
336: - Examples: Document type selection, frontmatter requirements
337: 
338: **Keep Markdown Prose When:**
339: - Explanatory text and conceptual overviews
340: - Narrative examples with context
341: - Best practices guidance
342: - Introductions and summaries

346: ## 6. DECISION LOGIC EXAMPLES
347: 
348: **Purpose**: Demonstrate how to convert markdown prose into structured decision logic.
349: 
350: ### Python Pseudo-Code: Mode Detection
351: 
352: **Before (Markdown Prose)**:
353: ```markdown
354: Check user input for mode indicators:
355: - If "$quick" is present, use quick mode with auto-scaling depth
356: - If "$ticket" is present, use ticket mode with depth 10
357: - Otherwise, use interactive mode with depth 10
358: ```
359: 
360: **After (Python Pseudo-Code)**:
361: ```python
362: def detect_mode(request):
363:     """Detect execution mode from user request markers"""
364: 
365:     if '$quick' in request:
366:         mode = 'quick'
367:         depth = 'auto_scale_1_to_5'
368:     elif '$ticket' in request:
369:         mode = 'ticket'
370:         depth = 'depth_10_rounds'
371:     else:
372:         # DEFAULT TO INTERACTIVE
373:         mode = 'interactive'
374:         depth = 'depth_10_rounds'
375: 
376:     return mode, depth
377: ```
378: 
379: ### Markdown Decision Tree: Frontmatter Requirements
380: 
381: **Before (Markdown Prose)**:
382: ```markdown
383: Different document types have different frontmatter requirements:
384: - SKILL.md files must have frontmatter with name, description, allowed-tools, and version
385: - Command files must have frontmatter with description and argument-hint
386: - Skill reference/asset files must have the 5-field block
387: - Knowledge files outside skill folders should not have frontmatter
388: - Spec files typically don't have frontmatter
389: ```
390: 
391: **After (Markdown Decision Tree)**:
392: ```

394: ├─> SKILL.md             → MUST have frontmatter (name, description, allowed-tools, version)
395: ├─> Command              → MUST have frontmatter (description, argument-hint, allowed-tools)
396: ├─> Skill Reference/Asset → MUST have the 5-field block (title, description,
397: │                           trigger_phrases, importance_tier, contextType)
398: ├─> Knowledge (outside skills) → MUST NOT have frontmatter (remove if present)
399: ├─> Spec                 → SHOULD NOT have frontmatter (suggest removal)
400: └─> README               → No specific requirement (usually none)
401: ```

403: ### Python Pseudo-Code: Validation Logic
404: 
405: **Before (Markdown Prose)**:
406: ```markdown
407: Validate the document structure:
408: 1. Check if required sections exist
409: 2. Verify section ordering is correct
410: 3. Ensure frontmatter is valid (if present)
411: ```
412: 
413: **After (Python Pseudo-Code)**:
414: ```python
415: def validate_document(doc, doc_type):
416:     """Validate document structure and content"""
417: 
418:     errors = []
419: 
420:     # Check required sections
421:     required_sections = get_required_sections(doc_type)
422:     for section in required_sections:
423:         if section not in doc.sections:
424:             errors.append(f"Missing required section: {section}")
425: 
426:     # Verify section ordering
427:     expected_order = get_section_order(doc_type)
428:     actual_order = [s.name for s in doc.sections]
429:     if actual_order != expected_order:
430:         errors.append(f"Section order incorrect. Expected: {expected_order}")
431: 
432:     # Validate frontmatter
433:     if doc.has_frontmatter:
434:         frontmatter_errors = validate_frontmatter(doc.frontmatter, doc_type)
435:         errors.extend(frontmatter_errors)
436: 
437:     return errors
438: ```

441: 
442: ## 7. WORKFLOW PATTERNS
443: 
444: **Purpose**: Show how to represent multi-step workflows using YAML structures.
445: 
446: ### YAML Pipeline: Document Creation Workflow
447: 
448: **Before (Markdown List)**:
449: ```markdown
450: 1. Analyze the request and determine document type
451: 2. Select appropriate template
452: 3. Populate template with content
453: 4. Validate structure and content
454: 5. Apply formatting standards
455: 6. Run quality checks
456: ```
457: 
458: **After (YAML Pipeline)**:
459: ```yaml

675: ## 9. TEMPLATE GUIDELINES
676: 
677: ### Naming Conventions
678: 
679: **File Names** (kebab-case required):
680: - Format: `[topic]-[type].md`
681: - Use hyphens, not underscores
682: - Lowercase only
683: - Descriptive and specific
684: - Examples:
685:   - ✅ `frontmatter-templates.md`
686:   - ✅ `validation-reference.md`
687:   - ✅ `config-examples.yaml`
688:   - ✅ `packaging-guide.md`
689:   - ❌ `templates.md` (too generic)
690:   - ❌ `FrontmatterTemplates.md` (wrong case)
691:   - ❌ `frontmatter_templates.md` (underscores are not canonical)
692: 
693: **Type-Specific Patterns**:
694: 
695: | Asset Type | Naming Pattern           | Kebab-case Examples          |
696: | ---------- | ------------------------ | ---------------------------- |
697: | Template   | `[content]-templates.md` | `frontmatter-templates.md`   |
698: | Reference  | `[topic]-reference.md`   | `emoji-reference.md`         |
699: | Example    | `[topic]-examples.md`    | `optimization-examples.md`   |
700: | Guide      | `[process]-guide.md`     | `packaging-guide.md`         |
701: | Checklist  | `[topic]-checklist.md`   | `validation-checklist.md`    |
702: 
703: **Section Names**:
704: - Use title case
705: - Be descriptive but concise
706: - Number if sequential: `1. Template Name`
707: 
708: ### Content Organization
709: 
710: **Progressive Disclosure**:
711: 1. **Introduction**: What this is, why it exists (1-2 sentences)
712: 2. **Sections**: Each covers one topic completely
713: 3. **Examples**: Show, don't just tell
714: 4. **Quick Reference**: Summary at end (optional)
715: 
716: **Section Structure**:
717: - **Purpose**: Why this section exists
718: - **Guidelines**: How to use the content
719: - **Template**: Copy-paste starting point
720: - **Example**: Complete working example
721: 
722: ### Formatting Standards
723: 
724: **Code Blocks**:
725: - Always specify language: ` ```yaml `, ` ```markdown `, ` ```bash `
726: - Include comments explaining non-obvious parts
727: - Show complete, runnable examples
728: - Use placeholder values that are obviously placeholders
729: 
730: **Placeholders**:
731: - Format: `[descriptive-name]` or `your-value-here`
732: - Examples:
733:   - ✅ `[skill-name]`, `[feature-description]`, `your-project-name`
734:   - ❌ `xxx`, `placeholder`, `FIXME`
735: 
736: **Lists**:
737: - Use `-` for unordered lists
738: - Use `1.` for ordered lists
739: - Nested lists indent by 2 spaces
740: - Keep items parallel in structure
741: 
742: **Tables**:
743: - Include header row
744: - Align consistently (usually left-aligned)
745: - Keep rows concise (1-2 lines)
746: - Use for comparisons or reference data
747: 
748: ### Writing Style
749: 
750: **Clarity**:
751: - Write for someone unfamiliar with your skill
752: - Define domain-specific terms on first use
753: - Use active voice: "Create the file" not "The file should be created"
754: - Be concise but complete
755: 
756: **Examples**:
757: - Every template should have a complete example
758: - Show real-world usage, not toy examples
759: - Include common variations
760: - Annotate non-obvious parts
761: 
762: **Consistency**:
763: - Use same terminology throughout
764: - Follow patterns from other assets in the skill
765: - Match style of SKILL.md
766: - Use consistent formatting
767:

771: 
772: **Before creating an asset file, verify**:

855: ## 12. ASSET MAINTENANCE
856: 
857: ### When to Update Assets
858: 
859: **Update asset files when**:
860: - New template variations emerge
861: - User feedback reveals confusion
862: - Standards or conventions change
863: - New use cases discovered
864: - Examples become outdated
865: 
866: **Version control**:
867: - Note significant changes in skill version bump
868: - Keep examples current with latest patterns
869: - Remove deprecated templates
870: - Add migration notes for breaking changes
871: 
872: ### Deprecation Strategy
873: 
874: **If removing a template**:
875: 1. Mark as deprecated in section header: `## DEPRECATED: Template Name`
876: 2. Explain why deprecated and what to use instead
877: 3. Keep for 1-2 skill versions (with deprecation warning)
878: 4. Remove after migration period

882: ## DEPRECATED: OLD TEMPLATE NAME
883: 
884: ⚠️ **This template is deprecated as of v3.0.0**

886: **Use instead**: `new-template-name.md` (see Section 2)

888: **Migration**: Replace X with Y in your existing files
889: ```

14: # Skill Asset File Templates - Creation Guidelines
15: 
16: Templates and guidelines for creating asset files in AI agent skills.
17: 
18: ## 1. OVERVIEW
19: 
20: ### Location & Naming
21: 
22: **Location:** `.skilled/skills/[skill-name]/assets/`
23: 
24: **Naming Convention:** kebab-case with the appropriate extension
25: 
26: | ✅ Valid Names | ❌ Invalid Names |
27: |---------------|-----------------|
28: | `frontmatter-templates.md` | `FrontmatterTemplates.md` (PascalCase) |
29: | `config-examples.yaml` | `config_examples.yaml` (snake_case) |
30: | `validation-checklist.md` | `ValidationChecklist.MD` (wrong case) |
31: | `emoji-reference.md` | `emojiReference.md` (camelCase) |
32: 
33: ### When to Create Assets
34: 
35: **Create an asset file when:**
36: - Templates users apply repeatedly
37: - Reference data >50 lines and self-contained
38: - Multiple examples of same pattern exist
39: - Lookup tables or decision matrices needed
40: - Template variations for different scenarios
41: 
42: **Keep in SKILL.md when:**
43: - Content <30 lines
44: - Tightly coupled to workflow logic
45: - Needs to be visible immediately (not progressive disclosure)
46: - Part of core instructions (RULES, WORKFLOW sections)
47: 
48: ---
49: 
50: ## 2. ASSET FILE TYPES
51: 
52: ### Template Files
53: **Purpose**: Provide copy-paste starting points for common tasks
54: 
55: **Naming**: `[content-type]-templates.md`
56: - Example: `frontmatter-templates.md`, `structure-templates.md`
57: 
58: **Structure**:
59: - One template per section
60: - Include field descriptions
61: - Show complete examples
62: - Explain when to use each template
63: 
64: **Use cases**:
65: - Document templates (SKILL.md, commands, knowledge files)
66: - Configuration templates (YAML, JSON)
67: - Code templates (functions, classes, modules)
68: 
69: ### Reference Files
70: **Purpose**: Provide lookup tables, decision trees, or reference data
71: 
72: **Naming**: `[topic]-reference.md`
73: - Example: `emoji-reference.md`, `validation-reference.md`
74: 
75: **Structure**:
76: - Tables or lists for quick lookup
77: - Decision matrices
78: - Classification systems
79: - Standards and conventions
80: 
81: **Use cases**:
82: - Emoji selection guides
83: - File type classifications
84: - Validation rule sets
85: - Naming conventions
86: 
87: ### Example Files
88: **Purpose**: Show working examples of skill outputs
89: 
90: **Naming**: `[topic]-examples.md`
91: - Example: `optimization-examples.md`, `skill-examples.md`
92: 
93: **Structure**:
94: - Before/after comparisons
95: - Annotated examples
96: - Multiple variations
97: - Anti-patterns to avoid
98: 
99: **Use cases**:
100: - Complete skill applications
101: - Common patterns
102: - Edge cases
103: - Quality standards
104: 
105: ### Guide Files
106: **Purpose**: Detailed how-to guides for complex processes
107: 
108: **Naming**: `[process]-guide.md`
109: - Example: `packaging-guide.md`, `distribution-guide.md`
110: 
111: **Structure**:
112: - Step-by-step instructions
113: - Troubleshooting sections
114: - Best practices
115: - Common pitfalls
116: 
117: **Use cases**:
118: - Multi-step processes
119: - Advanced techniques
120: - Workflow deep-dives
121: - Integration guides
122: 
123: ---
124: 
125: ## 3. DOCUMENT STRUCTURE
126: 
127: ### Title and Intro
128: 
129: **CRITICAL: The intro after the H1 title must be 1-2 SHORT sentences only.**
130: 
131: ```markdown
132: ---
133: title: [Title]
134: description: [One-line description - same as intro]
135: trigger_phrases:
136:   - "[distinctive phrase one]"
137:   - "[distinctive phrase two]"
138:   - "[distinctive phrase three]"
139: importance_tier: normal
140: contextType: general
141: version: 1.0.0.0
142: ---
143: 
144: # [Title]
145: 
146: [1-2 SHORT sentences only. Brief hook/summary. NO subsections, NO headers here.]
147: 
148: \## 1. OVERVIEW
149: 
150: ### Purpose
151: 
152: [Why this asset exists]
153: 
154: ### Usage
155: 
156: [How to use this asset - copy instructions, customization notes]
157: 
158: ---
159: 
160: \## 2. [Content Section]
161: 
162: [The actual template/checklist/snippet content]
163: 
164: ---
165: 
166: ## N. Related Resources (optional, if present must be last)
167: 
168: [Links to related files]
169: 
170: ```
171: 
172: Every asset file carries this full 5-field frontmatter block: the Skill Advisor harvests it as routing signal (3-8 lowercase multi-word `trigger_phrases` drawn from the doc's content, `importance_tier` defaults to `normal`, and `contextType` is one of `planning|research|implementation|general`). See [frontmatter-templates.md](../../../sk-create-frontmatter/assets/frontmatter-templates.md) for field rules.
173: 
174: > **WARNING: DO NOT duplicate content between intro and OVERVIEW section.**
175: > The intro is a hook. OVERVIEW provides the details.
176: 
177: #### GOOD Intro Structure
178: 
179: ```markdown
180: # Git Commit Templates
181: 
182: Copy the template that matches the change, fill the fields, and commit.
183: 
184: \## 1. OVERVIEW
185: 
186: ### Purpose
187: 
188: Uniform messages let a reader scan history by intent instead of by author.
189: 
190: ### Usage
191: 
192: Copy the appropriate template based on commit type...
193: 
194: ---
195: 
196: \## 2. COMMIT TEMPLATES
197: ...
198: ```
199: 
200: #### BAD Intro Structure (too long, has subsections)
201: 
202: ```markdown
203: # Git Commit Templates
204: 
205: Copy-paste templates for creating well-structured commit messages.
206: 
207: ### Core Principle    ← WRONG: No headers in intro!
208: Atomic commits with clear intent = maintainable history.
209: 
210: ### When to Use       ← WRONG: This belongs in OVERVIEW section!
211: - Creating new features
212: - Fixing bugs
213: 
214: ---
215: ```
216: 
217: ### Intro vs OVERVIEW Content Placement
218: 
219: | Content Type          | Intro (after H1) | OVERVIEW Section       |
220: | --------------------- | ---------------- | ---------------------- |
221: | 1-2 sentence summary  | ✅ YES            | ❌ NO (don't repeat)    |
222: | Core Principle        | ❌ NO             | ✅ YES (in Purpose)     |
223: | When to Use           | ❌ NO             | ✅ YES (in Purpose)     |
224: | How to copy/customize | ❌ NO             | ✅ YES (in Usage)       |
225: | Prerequisites         | ❌ NO             | ✅ YES (in Usage)       |
226: | Any H2/H3 subsections | ❌ NEVER          | ✅ YES                  |
227: 
228: ---
229: 
230: ## 4. STANDARD ASSET STRUCTURE
231: 
232: **Template**:
233: 
234: ````markdown
235: ---
236: title: Asset Title - Descriptive Subtitle
237: description: One-line description of what this asset provides
238: trigger_phrases:
239:   - "[distinctive phrase one]"
240:   - "[distinctive phrase two]"
241:   - "[distinctive phrase three]"
242: importance_tier: normal
243: contextType: general
244: version: 1.0.0.0
245: ---
246:

The README answers what outcome the skill delivers, when to reach for it, what it does not own and how to navigate its files. `SKILL.md` stays the runtime instruction surface. The README is the front door a person reads.
25: 
26: ### Identity Guidance (Purpose First)
27: 
28: The identity of a skill is the outcome it delivers. State that outcome in one plain sentence before naming tools.
29: Describe CLIs, commands, routing paths and reference files only after the outcome.
30: A README that opens with a tool name has not stated its identity.
31: 
32: The mcp-obsidian README states the outcome first: it makes AI use inside Obsidian effective.
33: It names the CLIs and MCP server later as delivery surfaces.
34: Repeat the outcome in the frontmatter description and the pitch.
35: The description supports a quick scan. The pitch opens the full README.
36: 
37: ### Usage
38: 
39: Copy the fillable scaffold in Section 6 into `.skilled/skills/[skill-name]/README.md`, then replace every placeholder with current behavior taken from the skill's real files. Keep the numbered ALL-CAPS section headers, the house style and the validator both require them. Drop any section that does not earn its place and renumber the rest.
40: 
41: ### Template Focus
42: 
43: The README gives people a human entry point, current capabilities and a clear route to supporting files. This template provides:
44: 
45: - A one-line pitch in a blockquote right after the H1, stating the outcome before any tool name.
46: - An identity guidance block that puts the delivered outcome ahead of the tooling.
47: - A capability section pattern for a skill's headline strengths, modeled on the pilot's Plugin Knowledge Layer.
48: - A dedicated HVR enforcement section with the banned forms and the scripted checks.
49: - Versioning conventions and a validation checklist that matches the pilot's gates.
50: 
51: ---
52: 
53: ## 2. SECTION MODEL
54: 
55: A skill README uses numbered ALL-CAPS H2 sections with `---` dividers between them. The default order:
56: 
57: | # | Section | Purpose | Keep When |
58: |---|---------|---------|-----------|
59: | 1 | AT A GLANCE | Four-row table a reader scans in five seconds | Always |
60: | 2 | OVERVIEW | What the skill is and what the reader gets first, then the optional problem narrative | Always (required by the validator) |
61: | 3 | QUICK START | The fastest path to a first result | Skill has commands, scripts or a workflow |
62: | 4 | HOW IT WORKS | The main workflow in prose, with a small Mermaid diagram for multi-step flows | Skill has non-obvious behavior worth explaining |
63: | 5 | INTEGRATION & NAVIGATION | When to use it, plus how it hands off to sibling skills | Readers can confuse it with a neighbor |
64: | 6 | TROUBLESHOOTING | The failure modes operators actually hit | Predictable issues exist |
65: | 7 | FAQ | The two to five questions readers keep asking | High-value answers exist |
66: | 8 | VERIFICATION | How you know the skill works | Skill ships a playbook or validation command |
67: | 9 | RELATED DOCUMENTS | Stable links out, `SKILL.md` first | Always when links exist |
68: 
69: `OVERVIEW` is the one required section. Its normalized name must appear as a numbered header so the validator finds it. Every other section is optional. A small utility skill might run four sections (AT A GLANCE, OVERVIEW, QUICK START, RELATED DOCUMENTS). A large orchestrator might run all nine. Match the count to the skill. Never pad to hit a number.
70: 
71: Inside OVERVIEW, start with `### What It Does`. Say what the skill is and what the reader gets.
72: Add up to two optional subsections after it.
73: Use `### Why This Skill Exists` only to name a current reader problem.
74: Add the capability section below when it earns a table.
75: 
76: ### Capability Section Pattern
77: 
78: When a skill has a headline strength, add a named capability section after What It Does.
79: Use one or two short sentences to say why the strength matters.
80: Use an analogy only when it clarifies the mechanism.
81: Name the section after its domain and add one table row per capability.
82: State the file or data the skill can operate on.
83: Avoid marketing claims. The prose explains why the capability matters. The table states what it does.
84: 
85: ```markdown
86: ### The Plugin Knowledge Layer
87: 
88: | Plugin | What the skill knows how to operate |
89: |---|---|
90: | **Beancount Ledger** | append and patch balanced transactions in the structured `.beancount` ledger |
91: | **Obsidian Tables** | edit `columns`, `rows` and `views` inside `.table.md` JSON payloads |
92: ```

94: ---
